I am 68 years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou County for 50 years. I did not finish school, but I know every inch of my 8 mu, and I know what this soil needs. My wife and I are the only ones left in the household, so I cannot afford to take risks or try fancy new methods. I stick to the wheat-maize rotation that has fed us for decades because it works.

This year, I will plant winter wheat on all 8 mu in October, right after the National Day. I will plough the field first to bury the maize stalks and break up the soil, because wheat needs a deep, loose bed to survive the winter. I buy hybrid wheat seeds from the county supply shop — they cost more than traditional seeds, but they give better yield and the stalks do not lodge easily. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as a base and then topdress with urea at the jointing stage. In total, I put down about 20 jin of nitrogen, 10 jin of phosphorus, and 6 jin of potassium per mu over the season. The well gives me water, so I will irrigate three times: before winter to protect the seedlings from freezing, at jointing when the wheat starts shooting up, and once more at grain filling. I will spray pesticide three times when I see aphids or rust start to appear, because if you wait too long, the whole field turns yellow. I expect about 500 kg per mu if the spring winds do not damage it.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I have to move fast. I will use rotary tillage to prepare the ground quickly for summer maize — there is no time to waste in double-cropping. I plant hybrid maize seeds right away. Maize loves nitrogen, especially at the big trumpet stage, so I will side-dress urea then. Total fertilizer for maize is about 18 jin nitrogen, 8 jin phosphorus, and 5 jin potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times: at seedling stage if it is too dry, at big trumpet when the ears are forming, and at filling. Two pesticide sprays should be enough to control corn borer and armyworm. If the autumn frost comes late, I can get 550 kg per mu.
